title: David Established: A Palace, a Family, and Two Victories
summary: Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen to build David a palace, and David recognizes that the LORD has established his kingdom for the sake of Israel. His family grows in Jerusalem. When the Philistines attack twice in the Valley of Rephaim, David asks God what to do each time, obeys, and wins, and his fame spreads to every land.
story: The chapter sits in an unexpected place. In 1 Chronicles 13 David's first attempt to bring the ark of God to Jerusalem ended in disaster when Uzzah was struck down, and the ark was left for three months at the house of Obed-edom. Chapter 15 will tell the second, successful attempt. Between the two, the Chronicler sets this short account of blessing: a palace, sons, and victories. In 2 Samuel 5 these same events come before the first ark attempt, so the Chronicler has moved them. The effect is to show, during the three months of waiting, that God had not turned against David. The king who learned the hard way that the holy God must be approached rightly is also the king whom God is plainly establishing. The chapter's last line, that the LORD made all nations fear him, sets up the great promise of chapter 17.
historical:
David ruled Israel from about 1010 to 970 BC, first from Hebron and then from Jerusalem, which he had taken from the Jebusites (1 Chronicles 11). Tyre, on the Phoenician coast north of Israel, was a wealthy trading city with access to the cedar forests of Lebanon, the prized building timber of the ancient Near East. A king named Hiram of Tyre also supplied Solomon for the temple (1 Kings 5), and historians have noticed that if the same Hiram helped both kings, his reign must have been long or this gift must have come late in David's reign. The Chronicler, like the writer of Samuel, arranges material by theme as much as by strict sequence, so the placement here doesn't settle the date.

The Philistines were Israel's great rivals in this period, a people settled on the southern coastal plain in cities such as Gaza, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath, and Ashkelon. As long as David was a vassal or a rival to Saul's house, they had tolerated him. Once he was anointed king over all Israel (verse 8), he was a threat, and they came looking for him. The Valley of Rephaim lies just southwest of Jerusalem, so the attack struck close to the new capital. Gibeon lay a few miles northwest of Jerusalem and Gezer farther west toward the coastal plain, so the rout in verse 16 drove the Philistines back down toward their own territory. The parallel in 2 Samuel 5:25 reads Geba rather than Gibeon.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, a gift of building materials and skilled workers from one king to another was diplomacy as much as generosity. It recognized the new king as a peer, opened trade, and assumed friendly relations. A palace of cedar was the visible sign that a ruler had arrived. Multiple wives were also a mark of royal status and alliance in that world, though the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:17 warned against it, and the later story of David's sons shows the cost.

Armies carried images of their gods into battle as a pledge of divine help, so abandoning them was a sign of total rout. In 2 Samuel 5:21 David and his men carry the idols off. The Chronicler adds that David ordered them burned, which is what Deuteronomy 7:5 and 7:25 require of images of foreign gods. The detail shows David keeping the law where Saul, in the Chronicler's telling, had failed to seek the LORD (1 Chronicles 10:13-14). The sign in the balsam trees (the tree's identification is uncertain) turns the rustling of leaves into the sound of God's own army marching ahead.
literary: The chapter has three panels. The first (verses 1-2) reports Hiram's gift and gives its meaning: David knew that the LORD had established him, and that his kingdom was exalted for the sake of His people Israel, not for David's own sake. The second (verses 3-7) is a short list of children born in Jerusalem, with Solomon, the future temple builder, named among them. The third (verses 8-17) tells two battles built on the same pattern: the Philistines raid, David inquires of God, God answers, David obeys, and victory follows. The repetition is the point. David doesn't assume that the first answer covers the second situation; he asks again and receives a different strategy. The place name ties back to chapter 13. There the LORD's anger broke out against Uzzah and the place was named Perez-uzzah; here God breaks out against Israel's enemies, and the place is named Baal-perazim, lord of breakthroughs.

outline.t: First battle: God bursts out at Baal-perazim
Second battle: the sound in the balsam trees

doctrines.note: David recognizes that his position is God's doing and that it exists for the sake of God's people. Chronicles consistently presents kingship as a gift held in trust, not a personal possession.

Twice David inquired of God before fighting. The contrast with Saul, who did not seek the LORD (1 Chronicles 10:14), is deliberate. Seeking God is one of the Chronicler's great themes, and here it is concrete: asking before acting, and asking again when circumstances repeat.
The Philistines' gods are left on the battlefield and burned. The gods that were supposed to protect them could not protect themselves, a point the psalm of chapter 16 will make in words.

words.note: Shaal, to ask or inquire. It is the ordinary verb for asking, used here for seeking God's direction before a decision. The name Saul (Shaul) comes from the same root, which gives the Chronicler's contrast an edge: the king whose name means asked-for did not ask, and David did.

Parats, to break through or burst out. It is the key word of chapters 13 to 15. The LORD burst out against Uzzah in 13:11; here God bursts out against the Philistines like water through a breach; in 15:13 David will explain the earlier outburst. The same holy power that endangers careless worship protects an obedient people.

Pachad, dread or terror. The chapter ends with the LORD causing the nations to dread David. The word often names the fear that falls on enemies when God acts for his people, as in the conquest accounts. The fear belongs to what God does, not to David's own reputation.

christ: David here is the king who asks his Father before he acts and wins because God goes out before him. The sound of marching in the treetops is a picture of the truth that the battle belongs to the LORD. The New Testament presents Jesus as David's greater son, and the Gospels show him in the same posture of dependence: praying before choosing the Twelve, withdrawing to pray before decisive moments, and saying that he does only what he sees the Father doing (John 5:19). The link here is a pattern rather than a prediction. Where David's victory spread his fame to every land, the church confesses that Christ's victory over sin and death is announced to all nations.
questions: David asked God twice about what looked like the same situation and got two different answers. Where are you tempted to repeat what worked before instead of seeking direction again?
Verse 2 says David's kingdom was exalted for the sake of God's people. How would it change your view of your own gifts or position to see them as held for others?
The Philistines brought their gods into battle and then abandoned them. What do people carry into life's battles as a source of security, and what happens to those things under pressure?
